rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The elution window and resolutions will guide subsequent window, slope, and temperature adjustments.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding composition and temperature fixed to test a faster fully resolved method and measure the critical pair’s slope response.
The 6-minute gradient retains full resolution with a minimum R of 2.46. Test a 4-minute gradient to shorten elution further while checking whether the first pair remains above R = 1.5.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Raise temperature at fixed gradient to test whether altered selectivity permits faster elution while retaining full resolution.

Heating weakened the critical first-pair separation, so test the lowest temperature with the shortest gradient to see whether cooler selectivity compensates for gradient compression. Injection 3 remains the fastest demonstrated method with maximum CRF.

Reduce gradient steepness by narrowing the organic window, targeting an increase in first-pair resolution from 1.23 to approximately 1.5–1.6. The final peak may elute during the hold, but this could still yield a faster fully resolved method than injection 3.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope that resolved every pair in injection 6. The stronger final solvent should accelerate the last peak, while the modest increase in starting organic tests whether first-pair resolution can be preserved.

Shift the window upward again at the same gradient slope to accelerate the last peak while aiming to preserve full resolution. Monitor the first pair for retention loss as the starting organic fraction rises.

Move the window up one more grid step at unchanged slope, since injection 8 preserved full resolution. The stronger endpoint should shorten the final hold elution while the first pair remains the key resolution check.

Increase starting organic by one step to advance the last peak while making the gradient slightly shallower. Check whether this preserves first-pair resolution before either early peak becomes effectively unretained.

Use the first pair’s resolution margin to test a modest temperature increase, shortening late retention without changing the gradient. A 5 °C step limits the selectivity risk observed with stronger heating.

Test the next starting-organic step at the cooler temperature that favors first-pair selectivity. This probes whether a narrower gradient can shorten elution further without compressing the early peaks below R = 1.5; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Return to phi0 = 0.30 to avoid the early-peak compression seen at 0.35, then test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This checks the thermal resolution boundary; if the first pair falls below 1.5, retain injection 11.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores first-pair resolution at 35 °C while keeping all peaks well within 10 minutes. This explores an alternative maximum-CRF method; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved choice.

The first pair barely responded to a shallower slope at phi0 = 0.30, suggesting insufficient initial retention. Lower phi0 one step to move both early peaks into the gradient and test whether full resolution can be recovered at 35 °C.

Reduce the gradient span by one grid step to raise the critical pair’s resolution from 1.42 toward 1.5. The stronger initial retention than at phi0 = 0.30 should allow better slope response, with ample time margin for the final peak.

Refine around injection 11, the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, by lowering the endpoint one step to test for additional resolution margin at modest time cost. Injection 16 is borderline despite its rounded CRF, so it is not a robust replacement.

Lower starting organic one step from injection 17 to keep the first peak farther from the unretained region while testing whether full resolution survives the slightly steeper gradient. Injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 18 to shorten final-peak retention and test the resolution boundary at this starting composition. The first pair’s small margin makes this a boundary check, with injection 11 retained as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a cooler, slightly shallower-gradient neighbor of injection 11 for greater first-pair resolution margin while retaining rapid elution. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a cooler, narrower-window method for additional first-pair resolution margin while keeping the first peak away from the unretained region. This seeks a robust maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 21 to shorten the final hold while retaining its favorable initial retention. The first-pair margin should accommodate this modest steepening, providing another fast maximum-CRF option.

Raise temperature one step from injection 21 to shorten late elution while testing whether its first-pair resolution margin remains sufficient. This refines a well-retained alternative near the maximum-CRF methods; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved choice.

Shift the starting organic upward one step from injection 23 to shorten elution while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Nearby results suggest full resolution is likely; injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated method attaining the maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to test a cooler neighbor expected to provide additional first-pair resolution margin while maintaining maximum CRF. Retain injection 11 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with all six peaks eluting by 2.58 minutes.
